pages.title: Making a cable safe to test
pages.for: Making a subsea cable safe to test, and safe to touch after every test. Each core is a long capacitor, and it may run beside a live string. So dead is not the same as safe.
pages.rule:
Identify → Isolated → Proved dead → Secured → Earthed
Talk to the far end before every change.
Earth both ends. Lift an earth only to connect a test.
After a test, check the set reads discharged. Use the discharge stick, then fit the earths.
Induced voltage grows with the neighbour's current, closeness and parallel length.

C = C per km × length
Q = C × V
E = ½ × C × V²
Off at the peak of U0, the usual trapped charge: E = C × U0²

traps.text: Taking proved dead as safe to touch. It only shows no voltage at that moment.
Forgetting that a cable beside a live one picks up voltage along its length.
traps.cite: Notes p.2; CIGRE TB on induced voltages (research)

traps.text: Lifting the earth straight after a discharge. Charge creeps back from the insulation.
Earthing one end only. The far end sits at the induced voltage.
traps.cite: CIGRE TB: shunted and locally earthed (research); notes p.2

traps.text: Leaving out the peak. ½ × C × U0² is half the energy at the peak.
traps.cite: Case assumption a.trapped; EPRI capacitor guide, J = ½CV² (research); IEEE TechNav, capacitive current breaks at a current zero, near peak charge (research)

pages.where: Before and after every test, at both ends of the cable. Your HV safety rules and the permit say who applies and lifts the earths.

pages.name: Do you still have it?
pages.task: String A is live in the same corridor. String B's cable from B01 to the OSS is isolated, and you have proved it dead at the OSS end. What must happen before anyone touches its cores?
pages.answer: Discharge it, then apply earths at both ends
pages.alt: Proved dead means no voltage at that moment. The core is still a capacitor, and String A can still induce a voltage on it. Discharging empties it. Earths at both ends hold it at earth while you work. The whole sequence is Identify, Isolated, Proved dead, Secured, Earthed.
options: Nothing more: it has been proved dead
Discharge it, then apply earths at both ends
Open the isolator at B01 as well, then start
pages.html: Proved dead means no voltage at that moment. The core is still a capacitor, and String A can still induce a voltage on it. Discharging empties it. Earths at both ends hold it at earth while you work. The whole sequence is Identify, Isolated, Proved dead, Secured, Earthed.

pages.name: What it is for
pages.text: From the middle out, the core's layers are conductor, inner semi-con, XLPE, outer semi-con, metal screen, aluminium foil and oversheath. Core resistance checks the conductor. IR and VLF check the XLPE between conductor and screen. The sheath test checks the oversheath, screen to earth. TDR uses conductor and screen as a pair.
pages.alt: Identify: the test points are known. Isolated: every energy source is disconnected. Proved dead: no voltage is verified. Secured: it is locked off and access is controlled. Earthed: earths are applied. If it is skipped Four main things set how badly a shock hurts: voltage, resistance, path and duration. At 55 V your body is about 10 000 Ω. So 55 V drives 5.50 mA. 50 mA or more is potentially fatal. Your body's resistance falls as the voltage rises. So a charged HV core drives far more current than that sum suggests.
pages.html:
• Identify: the test points are known.
  • Isolated: every energy source is disconnected.
  • Proved dead: no voltage is verified.
  • Secured: it is locked off and access is controlled.
  • Earthed: earths are applied.

If it is skipped

Four main things set how badly a shock hurts: voltage, resistance, path and duration. At 55 V your body is about 10 000 Ω. So 55 V drives 5.50 mA. 50 mA or more is potentially fatal. Your body's resistance falls as the voltage rises. So a charged HV core drives far more current than that sum suggests.

In a three-core subsea cable, armour wraps all three cores. Some designs use a lead sheath in place of the copper wires and foil.

Core resistance: The conductor, end to end.

IR: Conductor to screen, through the XLPE, at a steady d.c. voltage.

Sheath test: Screen to earth, through the oversheath.

VLF: Conductor to screen again, well above the working voltage.

TDR: Conductor and screen together, as a line a pulse runs along.

pages.name: The why
pages.text: A 1.00 km core holds 0.220 µF. Switched off at the peak of U0, 38 kV, it could hold 317.68 J. A longer core holds more. An earth drains it to zero. Lift the earth too soon and some charge creeps back from the insulation.
pages.alt: The conductor and the screen are two metal plates, with the XLPE between them. So every core is a capacitor. Capacitance grows with the area of the plates, so it grows with length. This cable has about 0.22 µF per km in each core. A charged core keeps its charge after it is disconnected. Its charge is Q = C × V. The energy it holds is E = ½ × C × V². While the core sits charged, some charge soaks into the insulation itself. An earth drains the conductor quickly. The charge in the insulation comes back out slowly. So a core earthed for a moment can build a voltage again.
pages.html:
The conductor and the screen are two metal plates, with the XLPE between them. So every core is a capacitor. Capacitance grows with the area of the plates, so it grows with length. This cable has about 0.22 µF per km in each core.

A charged core keeps its charge after it is disconnected. Its charge is Q = C × V. The energy it holds is E = ½ × C × V². While the core sits charged, some charge soaks into the insulation itself. An earth drains the conductor quickly. The charge in the insulation comes back out slowly. So a core earthed for a moment can build a voltage again.

A breaker breaks a cable's charging current as it passes through zero. That moment falls at the peak of the voltage. So a core switched off is usually left charged at the peak of U0.

U0 is its voltage between conductor and screen. The peak is √2 × U0, so E = ½ × C × (√2 × U0)² = C × U0². U0 is 38 kV for this 38/66 kV cable.

Capacitance0.220 µF
Most energy, off at the peak317.68 J

The charge that soaked into the XLPE has come back out. It has built a voltage on the core again.

It has recharged from the insulation. Earth it again and leave the earth on.

pages.name: Check
pages.task: A cable with no live neighbours has just had an insulation resistance test. You earth it for a moment, then lift the earth to connect the next lead. What can its core do?
pages.answer: Build a voltage again from charge in the insulation
pages.alt: The earth empties the conductor quickly. Charge soaked into the insulation comes out slowly and builds a voltage again. So re-earth it, and keep the earth on until the next lead is connected.
options: Stay at zero: the earth emptied it
Build a voltage again from charge in the insulation
Recharge only if its far end is still connected
pages.html: The earth empties the conductor quickly. Charge soaked into the insulation comes out slowly and builds a voltage again. So re-earth it, and keep the earth on until the next lead is connected.

pages.name: The live string beside it
pages.text: With only the OSS end earthed, the B01 end sits at the induced voltage. That is 96 V over 2.40 km, at the practice 40 V per km. Earth both ends and both are held at earth. A current circulates through the earths instead.
pages.alt: String A runs live in the same corridor. Its load current sets up a magnetic field. Where the cables run side by side, that field induces a voltage along String B's core. It works the way a transformer's primary drives its secondary. No connection is needed. The voltage grows with String A's current, how close the cables run and how far they run together. String A's voltage does not set it. The earthed screen keeps String A's electric field away from the core. So the magnetic coupling is the one that matters here. The induced voltage stands between the two ends of the core.
pages.html:
String A runs live in the same corridor. Its load current sets up a magnetic field. Where the cables run side by side, that field induces a voltage along String B's core. It works the way a transformer's primary drives its secondary. No connection is needed.

The voltage grows with String A's current, how close the cables run and how far they run together. String A's voltage does not set it. The earthed screen keeps String A's electric field away from the core. So the magnetic coupling is the one that matters here.

The induced voltage stands between the two ends of the core. Earth one end, and all of it appears at the other. Earth both ends, and it drives a current round through the earths instead.

Voltage at the B01 end96 V

String A's field induces 96 V along the 2.40 km run. Only the OSS end is earthed, so the B01 end stands at all 96 V.

Take 40 V per km as a practice value for String A at full load. It only gives the picture a number.

A fault or switching on String A can push this far higher without warning. Earth both ends before anyone works on the cable.

Lift an earth to connect a test, and that end stands at the induced voltage again. Treat the test end as live while String A runs.

pages.name: Worked example
pages.text: At 55 V your body takes 55 ÷ 10 000 = 5.50 mA. That is under 50 mA, but the figure holds only near 55 V. A 0.80 km core holds 0.22 × 0.80 = 0.176 µF. At the peak of U0, 38 kV, it could hold 0.176 × 10⁻⁶ × 38 000² = 254.14 J.
pages.alt: YOUR BODY, THEN A 0.80 KM CORE Your body at 55 V: I = V ÷ R = 55 ÷ 10 000 = 0.0055 A = 5.50 mA That is under 50 mA. But the 10 000 Ω holds only near 55 V. At HV your body's resistance is lower. A charged core is what would drive that current. Take a 0.80 km core of this cable, a practice length. C = 0.22 × 0.80 = 0.176 µF Switched off at the peak of U0: E = C × U0² = 0.176 × 10⁻⁶ × 38 000² = 254.14 J Leave out the peak and you get ½ × C × U0² = 127.07 J, half the energy at the peak.
pages.html:
Your body, then a 0.80 km core

Your body at 55 V: I = V ÷ R = 55 ÷ 10 000 = 0.0055 A = 5.50 mA

That is under 50 mA. But the 10 000 Ω holds only near 55 V. At HV your body's resistance is lower.

A charged core is what would drive that current. Take a 0.80 km core of this cable, a practice length.

C = 0.22 × 0.80 = 0.176 µF

Switched off at the peak of U0:

E = C × U0² = 0.176 × 10⁻⁶ × 38 000² = 254.14 J

Leave out the peak and you get ½ × C × U0² = 127.07 J, half the energy at the peak.

pages.name: Section A 1(a)
pages.task: (a) Determine the capacitance of one core of String B, from B01 to the OSS. Take 0.22 µF per km, a typical figure for this cable. On a real job, use the cable's own data sheet.
pages.alt: String B: the cable from B01 to the substation SCENARIO Commissioning tests on a newly laid 66 kV inter-array cable on an offshore wind farm. It runs 2.40 km from turbine B01 to the offshore substation (OSS), the last cable of string B. Three-core, 3 × 240 mm² copper, XLPE, 38/66 (72.5) kV, copper wire screens, armoured, with one field joint 1620 m from the OSS. A technician at each end, talking before every change. The live string A runs in the same corridor. One fault waits to be found. Every figure is a practice value unless it is cited.
pages.html:
String B: the cable from B01 to the substationScenario

Commissioning tests on a newly laid 66 kV inter-array cable on an offshore wind farm. It runs 2.40 km from turbine B01 to the offshore substation (OSS), the last cable of string B. Three-core, 3 × 240 mm² copper, XLPE, 38/66 (72.5) kV, copper wire screens, armoured, with one field joint 1620 m from the OSS. A technician at each end, talking before every change. The live string A runs in the same corridor. One fault waits to be found. Every figure is a practice value unless it is cited.

Take 0.22 µF per km, a typical figure for this cable. On a real job, use the cable's own data sheet.

Give it in µF, to 3 places.

C = 0.22 × 2.40 = 0.528 µF

The 0.528 µF agrees with the maker's charging current. In service at 50 Hz, 2π × 50 × 0.528 × 10⁻⁶ × 38 000 = 6.30 A. This cable's charging current is typically 2.6 A per km. 2.6 × 2.40 = 6.24 A.

pages.name: Section A 1(b)
pages.task: Once String B is in service, it will be switched off for maintenance. (b) Determine the most energy one core could hold if it were switched off at the peak of its phase voltage. U0 is 38 kV for this 38/66 kV cable.
pages.alt: CARRIED FORWARD (a) Capacitance of one core, B01 to OSS 0.528 µF Once String B is in service, it will be switched off for maintenance. Give it in joules. E = ½ × C × (√2 × U0)² = C × U0² E = 0.528 × 10⁻⁶ × 38 000² = 762.43 J That much energy can sit on a core that has been switched off and isolated. That is why the core is discharged and earthed before anyone touches it.
pages.html:
Carried forward
(a)Capacitance of one core, B01 to OSS0.528 µF

Once String B is in service, it will be switched off for maintenance.

Give it in joules.

E = ½ × C × (√2 × U0)² = C × U0²

E = 0.528 × 10⁻⁶ × 38 000² = 762.43 J

That much energy can sit on a core that has been switched off and isolated. That is why the core is discharged and earthed before anyone touches it.

pages.name: Section B
pages.task: Explain why a disconnected cable is treated as live until it has been tested, discharged and earthed.
pages.why: A model answer: A disconnected cable can still be dangerous. Each core and its screen form a long capacitor. So the cable can hold charge after it has been switched off or tested. Charge soaked into the insulation can come back out and recharge the conductor, even after it has been discharged. A live circuit running nearby can also induce a voltage on the cable with no connection to it. Proving dead only shows there is no voltage at that moment. It does not stop charge returning or being induced. So the cable is discharged, and earths are applied at both ends. They drain the charge and hold the core at earth while the work goes on.

pages.name: Changed numbers
pages.task: A core of the same type of cable runs 1.80 km. U0 is again 38 kV. Determine the most energy it could hold if it were switched off at the peak of U0.
pages.alt: Same method, new numbers. Give it in joules. C = 0.22 × 1.80 = 0.396 µF E = 0.396 × 10⁻⁶ × 38 000² = 571.82 J A shorter core has less capacitance, so it stores less. The discipline is the same.
pages.html:
Same method, new numbers. Give it in joules.

C = 0.22 × 1.80 = 0.396 µF

E = 0.396 × 10⁻⁶ × 38 000² = 571.82 J
